title: Organize your data
subtitle: How to convert a behavior data table into a BDM dataset
---

Many experimental design tools outputs a single data table that contains all the data collected during a study. If this is the case and you want to convert this data file to BDM, follow the steps below.

## Prerequisites
- Data file is CSV or any other format that can be read and manipulated.
- The data table contains all the necessary columns for BDM, including:
  - A unique identifier for each agent (the person or computational model that produced the data)
  - Cognitive tests or questionnaires names
  - Observations (e.g., responses, ratings, etc.)
  - Any other relevant metadata, e.g., timestamps, conditions, etc.


## Dataset folder

Create a new folder for your dataset, e.g., `my-dataset/`. You will probably use some internal project names for this folder, but it helps a lot with discoverability if you use a descriptive name and apply a common naming convention (e.g., as in git repository names: `lower-case`).

This `my-dataset/` is your dataset folder. Within this folder, create the following structure:

1. Create a `README.md` file in the main directory of the dataset folder. The file will contain human-readable description (as markdown) and machine-readable metadata of the dataset (as YAML front matter).
2. Create a `LICENSE` file in the main directory of the dataset folder. This file should contain the license under which the dataset is released. You can use the [Open Data Commons Open Database License (ODbL)](https://opendatacommons.org/licenses/odbl/) or any other license of [your choice](https://choosealicense.com/).
3. Create an `agents.csv` file in the main directory of the dataset folder. This file lists the agents in the dataset (BDM uses "agent" for both human participants and computational ones). The file should contain at least the following columns:
    - `agent_index`: the agent's index within this dataset, matching their folder name, e.g., `agent_001`, `agent_002` (see [Naming things](/spec/conventions/naming.qmd)).
    - `agent_id`: an identifier that stays with the agent across studies, if one is available.

## Data folder

Split your data table into one table per activity per agent (e.g., group the data by `['agent_id', 'task_name']`) and save it in the corresponding agent's folder as follows:

- For each table, create a `my-dataset/data/<AGENT>/<SESSION>/<ACTIVITY>/` folder, where `<AGENT>` is `agent_001`, `agent_002`, … , `<SESSION>` is `session_1`, `session_2`, … , and `<ACTIVITY>` is the name of the instrument used.
  - If there is only one session, create a single session folder, e.g., `my-dataset/data/agent_001/session_1/`. If there are multiple sessions, create one folder per session in the agent's folder.
- Store the data files in the corresponding activity's folder. The data file should be named as `response.csv` for the [Response table](../spec/trial/response.qmd) (the suffix `_1` means first attempt). For additional supplementary data, use the same naming format: `stimulus.csv` for the [Stimulus table](../spec/trial/stimulus.qmd), etc.
- If the agent ran the same activity more than once, all the runs go in the same file. Each row carries a `runtime_id` identifying the run it came from, and an `attempt` number; the runs themselves are listed in the agent's `studyflow_log.csv`.


## Studyflow
To describe your experiment, you can use the [Studyflow Modeler](https://behaverse.org/studyflow-modeler) to create a studyflow. It generates a `studyflow.xml` file that describes the planned activities and how agents move between them; place it in the root folder of your dataset.

:::{.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The studyflow describes what was *planned*; what each agent actually did is recorded in a `studyflow_log.csv` file at the root of that agent's folder—one row per activity, with its order, completion status, and any agent-specific details such as the condition they were assigned to. See [Studyflows](/spec/studyflows.qmd).
:::

## Instruments
- Create an instrument file for each task/questionnaire in the `instruments/` folder. Each instrument file should contain the following information:
    - Name of the instrument
    - Description of the instrument
    - Any other relevant metadata, e.g., questions, parameters, etc.
